before: Before fifteen days were up our renegade had already purchased an excellent vessel with room for more than thirty people. To make the transaction safe and give it cover, he thought it best to make, as he did, a voyage to a place called Shershel, twenty leagues from Algiers on the Oran side, where there is an extensive trade in dried figs. He made this voyage two or three times in company with the Tagarin already mentioned. (The Moors of Aragon are called Tagarins in Barbary, and those of Granada Mudéjares; but in the Kingdom of Fez they call the Mudéjares Elches, and they are the people the king mostly employs in war.) Each time he passed with his vessel he anchored in a cove not two crossbow shots from the garden where Zoraida was waiting. There the renegade, together with the two Moorish lads who rowed, used to station himself on purpose, either saying his prayers or rehearsing what he meant to do for real. He would also go to Zoraida's garden and ask for fruit, which her father gave him, not knowing him. But although, as he afterwards told me, he tried to speak to Zoraida and tell her who he was, and that by my orders he was to take her to the land of the Christians so she might feel reassured, he had never been able to: Moorish women do not allow themselves to be seen by any Moor or Turk unless their husband or father bids them; with Christian captives they permit freedom of intercourse and communication, even more than might be considered proper. For my part I would have been sorry if he had spoken to her, since it might have alarmed her to find her affairs being discussed by renegades. But God, who ordered things otherwise, gave our renegade no opportunity for his well-meant attempt. Seeing how safely he could go to Shershel and back, anchoring when and where and how he liked, and that the Tagarin his partner had no will but his — and now that I was ransomed, all we needed was to find some Christians to row — he told me to look out for any I would be willing to take with me, beyond those who had been ransomed, and to engage them for the next Friday, which he had set for our departure. So I spoke to twelve Spaniards, all stout rowers and the sort who could most easily slip out of the city; but it was no easy matter to find that many just then, because there were twenty ships out cruising and they had taken all the rowers with them. These would not have been found if it had not been that their master had stayed at home that summer without going to sea, in order to finish a galliot he had on the stocks. I said nothing more to these men than that the next Friday in the evening they were to come out stealthily one by one and hang about Hadji Morato's garden, waiting for me until I came. I gave each one these directions separately, with orders that if they saw any other Christians there, they were to say nothing to them except that I had directed them to wait at that spot.
